Arthur Waley was a British translator and orientalist whose renderings of Chinese and Japanese classics introduced English readers to East Asian literary traditions. Over fifty years, he produced some thirty books of translation, establishing a standard for how Chinese and Japanese verse and prose could be rendered into elegant, readable English.

Waley was self-taught in Chinese and Japanese. He began at the British Museum cataloguing Oriental manuscripts, and he developed his linguistic abilities through immersion in texts rather than formal training. His translation of Murasaki Shikibu's The Tale of Genji, completed between nineteen twenty-one and nineteen twenty-eight, was the first complete English version and remains canonical. He rendered the eleventh-century court narrative into flowing, accessible English. He also translated The Dream of the Red Chamber, Cao Xueqin's eighteenth-century novel, capturing its episodic structure and domestic intricacy. The translation made this Chinese masterpiece available to English readers for the first time.

Waley translated hundreds of Chinese poems, particularly from the Tang and Song dynasties, into English free verse that captured the suggestiveness and imagistic precision of classical Chinese poetry without forcing rhyme. He was known for readability and elegance rather than literal fidelity. Modern scholars note he sometimes romanticized or simplified Chinese and Japanese syntax to suit English taste. Throughout his career, Waley declined academic positions to remain independent. He worked as a translator and cultural intermediary, writing essays on East Asian aesthetics and philosophy alongside his translations. His versions remained the standard for decades, and though later scholars produced more literal and academically rigorous translations, Waley's remain the most widely read and cited among general audiences.
